paper_title: Geo-EEG: Towards the Use of EEG in the Study of Urban Behaviour
abstract: In this paper, we present how mobile electroencephalography, or mobile EEG, is becoming a relevant tool of urban studies, including among others, spatial cognition, architecture, urban design and planning. Mobile EEG is a research methodology that requires tightly controlled experiments and complicated analytical tools, but it is increasingly used beyond the clinical and research context to monitor brain function and cognition in real world. It is used to unravel our understanding of the neural processes that enable spatial perception and cognition, while is also applied to the study of psychological transactions between people and the environment, for example to gauge the effects of urban or natural environments on the emotional state of pedestrians. In the near future, mobile EEG could be integrated in the research on cities as a tool to understand the cognitive foundations of urban movement, assess the psychological impact of environments on individuals, or target interventions to improve the quality of the urban environment. In this paper we review relevant research with mobile EEG, as well as the background and methodological issues arising in such projects.
methodology: Psychophysiological indicators (heart-rate (HR), skin conductance (SC), cortisol levels)
Crowdsourcing (e.g., Mappiness app, Place Pulse, Urban gems)
Mobile applications (apps) for geo-annotation of behavioral observations, delivering instructions, and wayfinding aids (maps)
EEG signal analysis techniques: Event Related Potential (ERP), frequency and power analysis (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, theta bands)
Time-synchronization of neural activity, stimuli, and external events using tools like Lab Streaming Layer
sample: Large-scale data sources (GPS, social media) with sample sizes exceeding targeted studies.
Roe et al. (2013) laboratory study: participants looked at 15 images.
Aspinall et al. (2013) naturalistic experiment: 12 participants.
Mavros et al. (2015) pilot study: individuals with visual impairments compared to sighted participants.
Roe and Aspinall (2011): adults with good or poor mental health.
Ward Thomson and colleagues (2013): residents in several deprived communities in Scotland.
manipulated_features: Urban vs. natural environments (e.g., busy street vs. park, green space zones, low-traffic vs. heavy-traffic streets, rural vs. urban settings)
Environmental stressors (noise, air pollution, traffic levels)
Building form, color, texture, street activity (in VR simulations)
Navigation task difficulty (active vs. passive navigation, shortest path vs. scenic route, directed wayfinding with path planning)
Design of spaces (e.g., 'well-designed places with good ambience')
outcomes: Brain function and activity (EEG signals, power in alpha, beta, gamma, delta, theta frequency bands)

Cognitive processes (spatial perception, spatial cognition, spatial memory, working memory load, attention, navigation task difficulty, navigational performance, route choice, spatial decision-making, processing of landmarks)
Emotional states (arousal, stress, relaxation, frustration, engagement, meditation, mood, wellbeing, happiness)
Physiological indicators (heart rate, skin conductance, cortisol levels)
Behavioral data (movement patterns, route deviations, walking patterns, mobility patterns, activity rates, accident rates)
User intent (in Brain Computer Interface applications)
Environmental preferences (attractiveness, quietness, happiness of urban images)
key_findings: Mobile EEG is becoming a relevant tool for urban studies, extending beyond clinical/research contexts to monitor brain function and cognition in real-world environments.
Alpha activity increases with eyes closed or relaxation; beta increases with alertness/cognitive demands; delta with deep sleep; theta with drowsiness and is associated with navigational tasks.
Research-grade mobile EEG systems are superior, but commercial devices like Emotiv EPOC can be sufficient for certain experiments, especially with electrode modifications (Debener et al. 2012).

The hippocampus is critical for spatial memory and creating mental representations of space; its volume correlates with better performance in learning new environments (Maguire et al. 2003; Schinazi et al. 2013).

Theta frequency oscillations are related to encoding and retrieval of spatial information in the animal hippocampus (O'Keefe and Burgess 1999) and reflect working memory load, episodic memory (Mitchell et al. 2008), and navigation task difficulty/performance in humans (Bischof and Boulanger 2003; Kober and Neuper 2011).

Active navigation, requiring mental representations, shows different EEG patterns (short bursts of theta activity, increased theta power) compared to passive following (Bischof and Boulanger 2003; Havranek et al. 2012).
Increased theta activity occurs near decision points during navigation (Bischof and Boulanger 2003).
Theta activity correlates with participants' accuracy in navigation tasks (Kober and Neuper 2011), suggesting EEG can measure navigation difficulty.
Different EEG oscillation patterns are observed when landmarks of interest are in view versus irrelevant ones (Weidemann et al. 2009).
Increased EEG responses to landmarks were associated with taking longer paths and poorer navigational performance in virtual environments (Kober and Neuper 2011).

Virtual Reality (VR) navigation differs from real-world navigation; theta oscillations are attenuated in VR (animal studies), and VR lacks self-motion information from vestibular/proprioceptive cues (Taube et al. 2013). VR participants were less accurate in estimating bearing to locations (Waller and Greenauer 2007).
People often do not take the shortest path in urban navigation, instead using criteria like safety, pleasantness, aesthetics, complexity, and prior knowledge (Manley et al. 2015).
Pedestrians often deviate from planned routes, changing strategies opportunistically during a walk (Hölscher et al. 2011).
Natural scenes elicit increased power at the alpha frequency band, indicative of relaxation (Ulrich 1981).
People recuperate faster from stressors and are 'immunized' against future stressor tasks when exposed to vegetation (Parsons et al. 1998; Ulrich et al. 1991).
Living in proximity to green space has a positive effect on salivary cortisol levels (Ward Thomson et al. 2013).

Pilot mobile EEG studies found lower frustration, engagement, and arousal, and higher meditation when moving into green space zones, and higher engagement when moving out of them (Aspinall et al. 2013).
Emotional responses to natural or urban environments differ between passive (watching images) and active (walking outdoors) experiments.

A pilot study with visually impaired participants suggested differences in emotional experiences compared to sighted individuals, and EEG could localize negatively impacting areas (Mavros et al. 2015).
Walks in rural environments are particularly beneficial for individuals with poor mental health (Roe and Aspinall 2011).
Cycling in London provides health benefits even after controlling for risk factors (Woodcock et al. 2014).
theories_referenced: Restorative theory (Ulrich et al. 1991; Parsons and Tassinary 2002; Roe and Aspinall 2011)
Anchor-point hypothesis of spatial cognition (Couclelis et al. 1987)
Cognitive maps (Garling 1989; Golledge 1999; Kitchin and Blades 2002)
mechanisms: Neural processes in the hippocampal formation (place cells, grid cells, head direction cells) integrate information from multiple sensory cues to create coherent spatial representations (Burgess 2008).
Theta oscillations in the brain reflect working memory load and active navigation, indicating cognitive effort and spatial processing.
Psychological events are assumed to have a physiological referent, meaning mental states are reflected in measurable physiological changes (Cacioppo et al. 2000).
Natural environments may reduce attentional demands, leading to restoration of mental capacity.
Aesthetic preference for natural environments contributes to positive psychological outcomes.
Evolutionary dispositions may predispose humans to find natural environments restorative.
Brain oscillations (e.g., alpha for relaxation, theta for cognitive load) directly reflect mental states and cognitive processes.
limitations: EEG is generally restricted to studying neural activity close to the surface of the skull (cerebral cortex) due to the 'volume conductor' phenomenon, though 3D source reconstruction can partially address this (da Silva and F 2009).
fMRI and MEG equipment are bulky, noisy, and impose posture constraints on participants.
Traditional EEG systems required large equipment and complicated cable arrangements, limiting application beyond the laboratory.
Commercial mobile EEG devices typically have fewer electrodes and are less precise than research-grade systems.
Exact EEG classification algorithms for commercial devices (e.g., Emotiv's Affectiv metrics) are often proprietary and not peer-reviewed.

Virtual Reality (VR) environments are considered 'radically different' from real environments, lacking self-motion information from vestibular or proprioceptive cues, which may alter neural activity (Taube et al. 2013).
Naturalistic experiments face methodological challenges due to uncontrolled and uncontrollable conditions, making it difficult to establish accurate timing of responses to stimuli or environments.
Confounding factors in real-world settings (e.g., traffic, crowds, loud noises, accidental stumbles) must be registered and accounted for during data analysis.
GPS accuracy within city areas can be unreliable for precise participant location tracking.
Salivary cortisol levels change slowly and are not ideal for capturing short-term stress reduction in nature exposure experiments (Tyrväinen et al. 2014).
Pilot studies often involve small sample sizes, requiring larger samples and diverse environmental contexts for generalizability.
Combining various hardware and software tools for mobile EEG experiments introduces complexity.
Ethical questions arise regarding responsive environments that constantly mutate based on users' brain states, concerning agency and intentionality.
design_implications: Mobile EEG can be integrated into urban studies to understand cognitive foundations of urban movement, assess psychological impacts of environments, and target interventions to improve urban quality.
Findings can guide urban design and planning by indicating how spaces affect mood and cognitive states, helping create more pedestrian-friendly and 'walkable' cities.
EEG can be used as a diagnostic tool to localize urban areas that negatively impact individuals, informing design improvements.
Understanding the restorative effects of natural environments can inform policy and design to maximize mental health benefits of urban green spaces.
Mobile EEG can evaluate environmental design interventions and assess how spaces function affectively.
The technology can support a user-centric, inclusive approach to understanding life in cities, especially for diverse user groups like older people or those with visual impairments.

Research into responsive environments suggests possibilities for architectural installations that adapt to users' mental or emotional states, potentially enhancing user experience or providing assistive functions (e.g., controlling ambient lighting).
